claim: Perception of number and space are tightly intertwined.
source: Perception of number and space are tightly intertwined.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and is established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The intertwining of number and space perception is due to 'cortical recycling', where numerosity processing takes over circuits originally processing space.
source: It has been proposed that this is due to 'cortical recycling', where numerosity processing takes over circuits originally processing space.
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal cited from the literature.

claim: Visual motion direction adapts nonsymbolic numerosity perception, giving rise to a repulsive aftereffect.
source: We describe a new phenomenon in which visual motion direction adapts nonsymbolic numerosity perception, giving rise to a repulsive aftereffect: motion to the left adapts small numbers, leading to overestimation of numerosity, while motion to the right adapts large numbers, resulting in underestimation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from the study.

claim: Motion to the left adapts small numbers, leading to overestimation of numerosity.
source: motion to the left adapts small numbers, leading to overestimation of numerosity
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the adaptation experiments.

claim: Motion to the right adapts large numbers, resulting in underestimation of numerosity.
source: motion to the right adapts large numbers, resulting in underestimation
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the adaptation experiments.

claim: The reference frame of the motion direction-numerosity cross-adaptation effect is spatiotopic.
source: The reference frame of this effect is spatiotopic.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 6.

claim: Motion direction-numerosity cross-adaptation may occur in a homolog of area LIP.
source: Together with the tuning properties of the effect this suggests that motion direction-numerosity cross-adaptation may occur in a homolog of area LIP.
evidence: This is inferred from the tuning properties and reference frame data, combined with knowledge of LIP properties.

claim: 'Cortical recycling' expands but does not obliterate the functions originally performed by the recycled circuit.
source: 'Cortical recycling' thus expands but does not obliterate the functions originally performed by the recycled circuit, allowing for shared computations across domains.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Small numbers are mapped to the left and large numbers are mapped to the right on the mental number line.
source: Our perception of numerosity and space are tightly interrelated, as evidenced by the 'mental number line', where small numbers are mapped to the left and large numbers are mapped to the right (Dehaene et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The spatial arrangement of numbers is evident in preverbal infants.
source: This spatial arrangement of numbers is evident in preverbal infants (de Hevia and Spelke, 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The spatial arrangement of numbers is evident in non-human primates.
source: non-human primates (Drucker and Brannon, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The spatial arrangement of numbers is evident in birds.
source: even birds (Rugani et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The mental number line has a deep evolutionary heritage.
source: suggesting a deep evolutionary heritage of the mental number line
evidence: This is inferred from the cross-species evidence cited.

claim: The mental number line can be influenced by cultural practice.
source: although there is evidence that it can be influenced by cultural practice (Shaki and Fischer, 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Number-space interactions are attributed to the fact that the neural bases of numerical and space processing both localize to parietal cortex.
source: Number-space interactions are attributed to the fact that the neural bases of numerical and space processing both localize to parietal cortex (Hubbard et al., 2005)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Parietal lesions disrupt both numerical and spatial processing.
source: as evidenced by the fact that parietal lesions disrupt both numerical and spatial processing (Zorzi et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The co-localization of numerical and spatial processing is the result of 'cortical recycling' during evolution or normal development.
source: It has been suggested that this co-localization is the result of 'cortical recycling' during evolution or normal development (Anderson, 2010; Dehaene and Cohen, 2007)
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citations.

claim: Numerical cognition builds upon circuits that originally process space because the computations used to gauge target coordinates or transform reference frames can also be used for operations on numbers.
source: i.e., numerical cognition builds upon circuits that originally process space, because the computations that are used to gauge target coordinates or to transform reference frames can also be used for operations on numbers.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation from the literature.

claim: Motion can literally move us up and down the mental number line.
source: Thus, motion can literally move us up and down the mental number line.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings showing motion direction affects numerosity perception.

claim: Numerosity coopts circuits encoding space.
source: This indicates that numerosity coopts circuits encoding space.
evidence: This is inferred from the cross-adaptation findings.

claim: Recycled numerosity processing circuits remain sensitive to purely spatial features.
source: Thus, recycled numerosity processing circuits indeed remain sensitive to purely spatial features.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: 'Cortical recycling' augments but does not obliterate the spatial capacities of parietal circuits.
source: This shows that 'cortical recycling' augments but does not obliterate the spatial capacities of parietal circuits.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Parietal circuits that process number contain neurons that respond to motion.
source: Because the parietal circuits that process number are known to also contain neurons that respond to motion (Colby et al., 1993; Fanini and Assad, 2009)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Adaptation systematically reduces the responsivity of neurons that encode the adapted feature, leading to an overshoot of activity in neurons that respond to the opposite feature.
source: Classically, adaptation is thought to systematically reduce the responsivity of neurons that encode the adapted feature, leading to an overshoot of activity in neurons that respond to the opposite feature.
evidence: This is established knowledge about adaptation mechanisms.

claim: Adaptation typically results in a perceptual aftereffect in which subjects perceive the opposite of what they have been adapted to.
source: This typically results in a perceptual aftereffect in which subjects perceive the opposite of what they have been adapted to (Solomon and Kohn, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In the classical motion aftereffect, subjects perceive leftwards motion after being adapted to rightwards motion.
source: For example, in the classical motion aftereffect (MAE), subjects perceive leftwards motion after being adapted to rightwards motion (Levinson and Sekuler, 1976)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: In numerosity adaptation, subjects underestimate the numerosity of dots after being adapted to large quantities.
source: in numerosity adaptation, subjects underestimate the numerosity of dots after being adapted to large quantities (Burr and Ross, 2008)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: If the same population of neurons coded for motion direction and number, adaptation to leftwards motion should lead to subsequent overestimation of numerosity.
source: In particular, we hypothesized that if the same population of neurons coded for motion direction and number, adaptation to leftwards motion should lead to subsequent overestimation of numerosity
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: If the same population of neurons coded for motion direction and number, adaptation to rightwards motion should lead to underestimation of numerosity.
source: while adaptation to rightwards motion should lead to underestimation, reflecting a repulsive aftereffect
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: If number and motion direction were coded by different neurons, a cross-adaptation effect would not be expected.
source: In contrast, if number and motion direction were coded by different neurons, a cross-adaptation effect would not be expected, even if those neurons co-localized to the same brain area.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on theoretical reasoning.

claim: Adaptation to rightward motion led subjects to perceive the test cloud as relatively less numerous than adaptation to leftwards motion (mean difference in PSE 7.12 dots, t(10)=2.555, p=0.029, dHedges=0.953).
source: Adaptation to rightward motion led subjects to perceive the test cloud as relatively less numerous than adaptation to leftwards motion (mean difference in PSE 7.12 dots, t(10)=2.555, p=0.029, dHedges=0.953)
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Motion direction exclusively affected the PSE but not psychometric slopes in Experiment 1.
source: Motion direction exclusively affected the PSE but not psychometric slopes (mean difference -0.009, t(10)=−1.038, p=0.324, dHedges=−0.307).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: All psychometric functions are shifted to the right because of strong, inevitable adaptation effects of large numerosities and/or texture density that cause subjects to underestimate consecutively presented dot clouds.
source: Note that all psychometric functions are shifted to the right because of strong, inevitable adaptation effects of large numerosities (Burr and Ross, 2008) and/or texture density (Durgin, 2008) that cause subjects to underestimate consecutively presented dot clouds
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data based on prior knowledge from cited studies.

claim: When adapting with numerosities smaller than the probe (166 dots), subjects overestimate the number of dots in the test cloud.
source: When adapting with numerosities smaller than the probe (166 dots), subjects overestimate the number of dots in the test cloud (Burr and Ross, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to prior work.

claim: The PSE after leftward motion adaptation was smaller than after rightward motion adaptation in Experiment 2 (mean difference 15.85 dots; t(9)=4.523, p=0.001, dHedges=1.017).
source: the PSE after leftward motion adaptation was smaller than after rightward motion adaptation (Figure 2c; mean difference in PSE 15.85 dots; t(9)=4.523, p=0.001, dHedges=1.017)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 2c.

claim: There were no effects of motion direction on psychometric slopes in Experiment 2.
source: Again, there were no effects on slopes (mean difference −0.123, t(9)=−0.755, p=0.469, dHedges=−0.313).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Leftward motion more strongly adapts neurons coding for small numbers than rightward motion, causing a stronger repulsive aftereffect and thus increased overestimation.
source: Together, this indicates that leftward motion more strongly adapts neurons coding for small numbers than rightward motion, causing a stronger repulsive aftereffect and thus increased overestimation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings in Experiments 1 and 2.

claim: Rightward motion led to an overestimation of numerosity (a leftward shift of the PSE) in Experiment 3.
source: Rightward motion led to an overestimation of numerosity (a leftward shift of the PSE)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: Leftward motion led to underestimation of numerosity (a rightward shift of the PSE) in Experiment 3.
source: while leftward motion led to underestimation (a rightward shift of the PSE) (mean difference right vs. left PSE -2.08, t(9)=−2.47, p=0.035, dHedges=−0.707)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 3.

claim: There were no effects of motion direction on psychometric slopes in Experiment 3.
source: There were no effects on slopes (mean difference 0.007, t(9)=1.001, p=0.342, dHedges=0.351).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The smaller effect size in Experiment 3 compared to the adaptation experiments is likely due to the shorter exposure to motion direction (600 ms vs. 5000 ms).
source: The smaller effect size than in the adaptation experiments is likely due to the shorter exposure to motion direction (600 ms vs. 5000 ms).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design differences.

claim: Motion direction affects the perception of large as well as small numerosities.
source: Together, Experiments 1–3 demonstrate that motion direction affects the perception of large as well as small numerosities
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiments 1-3.

claim: The interaction between motion direction and numerosity can be revealed by repulsive aftereffects but does not depend on them.
source: and that this interaction can be revealed by repulsive aftereffects but does not depend on them, as it is also observed directly, i.e., in the absence of adaptation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiments 1-3.

claim: None of the 11 subjects tested in Experiment 4 perceived illusory motion in the test/probe stimuli.
source: None of the 11 subjects we tested perceived illusory motion in the test/probe stimuli (Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 4.

claim: The cross-adaptation aftereffect on numerosity directly arises from motion direction adaptation and is not mediated by a classical MAE.
source: This demonstrates that the cross-adaptation aftereffect on numerosity directly arises from motion direction adaptation, and is - like other high-level MAEs (Whitney and Cavanagh, 2003) - not mediated by a classical MAE.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings in Experiment 4 and comparison to prior work.

claim: Attention is not drawn in the direction of a repulsive classical MAE during the presentation of the test cloud.
source: This also speaks against the notion that attention could be drawn in the direction of a repulsive classical MAE during the presentation of the test cloud, thus shifting the focus of attention up or down the number line.
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of classical MAE in Experiment 4.

claim: The first stage of number processing in monkeys is in the intraparietal sulcus (IPS), specifically in areas LIP and VIP.
source: In monkeys, the first stage of number processing is in the intraparietal sulcus (IPS), specifically in areas LIP and VIP (Nieder and Dehaene, 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Neurons in monkey area LIP show monotonic increases and decreases in firing rate with the number of items in a display.
source: Such broad tuning curves for numerosity have been found in monkey area LIP, where neurons show monotonic increases and decreases in firing rate with the number of items in a display (Roitman et al., 2007)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Neurons in monkey area LIP are sensitive to motion direction.
source: and are also sensitive to motion direction (Fanini and Assad, 2009)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: LIP is thought to correspond to an intermediate analog representation of numerosity before the cardinal representation of number arises downstream in area VIP.
source: LIP is thought to correspond to an intermediate analog representation of numerosity before the cardinal representation of number arises (Dehaene and Changeux, 1993; Verguts and Fias, 2004) downstream in area VIP
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Area VIP is sensitive to motion.
source: which is also sensitive to motion (Colby et al., 1993)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Numerosity neurons in area VIP show much narrower tuning functions than those in LIP.
source: but where numerosity neurons show much narrower tuning functions (Nieder and Dehaene, 2009)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Adapting and probing with the same number of dots (30 in Experiment 5) did not lead to a significant motion direction-specific aftereffect.
source: In contrast, we found that adapting and probing with the same number of dots (30 in Experiment 5) did not lead to a significant motion direction-specific aftereffect (mean difference right vs. left −3.69, p=0.92, Wilcoxon signed rank test, one-sided; Bayesian posterior probability <0.18%).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from Experiment 5.

claim: The presence of a strong adaptation effect when adapting with 400 and testing with 30 dots and the absence of an adaptation effect when adapting and testing with 30 dots together indicate that motion direction-numerosity cross-adaptation may arise in a human homolog of area LIP.
source: The presence of a strong adaptation effect when adapting with 400 and testing with 30 dots and the absence of an adaptation effect when adapting and testing with 30 dots together indicate that motion direction-numerosity cross-adaptation may arise in a human homolog of area LIP.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings in Experiments 1 and 5, combined with knowledge of LIP properties.

claim: The IPS serves to convert retinotopic coordinates prevalent in early visual areas into eye-, head-, and world-centered frames of reference.
source: A second characteristic of the neural circuitry in the IPS is that it serves to convert retinotopic coordinates prevalent in early visual areas into eye-, head-, and world-centered frames of reference.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IPS function.

claim: Areas LIP and VIP both contain neurons with eye- and head-centered coordinates.
source: In particular, areas LIP and VIP both contain neurons with eye- and head-centered coordinates (Duhamel et al., 1997; Mullette-Gillman et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Neurons in area LIP have spatially restricted receptive fields, each covering only a portion of the visual world.
source: while neurons in area LIP have spatially restricted receptive fields, each covering only a portion of the visual world
evidence: This is established knowledge about LIP properties.

claim: Number-sensitive neurons in area VIP respond to stimuli distributed over the entire visual field.
source: number-sensitive neurons in area VIP, the next stage of number processing, respond to stimuli distributed over the entire visual field (Nieder and Dehaene, 2009)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Cross-adaptation between motion direction and number occurs even in the presence of two intervening saccades.
source: Figure 5 shows that cross-adaptation between motion direction and number occurs even in the presence of two intervening saccades, replicating Experiment 1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 6 shown in Figure 5.

claim: Cross-adaptation takes place in a spatiotopic, not retinotopic frame of reference.
source: the results of Experiment 6 show that cross-adaptation takes place in a spatiotopic, not retinotopic frame of reference
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from Experiment 6.

claim: Cross-adaptation is restricted to the spatiotopic location of the stimulus and does not extend over the full field of view.
source: but is restricted to the spatiotopic location of the stimulus and does not extend over the full field of view (motion direction × reference frame interaction, F(3,15)=4.58, p=0.018, η2=0.478)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from Experiment 6.

claim: Only the 'same location' and the 'spatiotopic' condition in Experiment 6 were significantly different from zero.
source: Only the 'same location' and the 'spatiotopic' condition were significantly different from zero (both p=0.015, Wilcoxon signed rank tests)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from Experiment 6.

claim: The 'retinotopic' and 'full field' conditions in Experiment 6 were not significantly different from zero.
source: while the 'retinotopic' and 'full field' condition were not (p=0.71 and p=0.84, respectively)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis from Experiment 6.

claim: Bayesian statistics confirmed that there was overwhelming evidence for an effect in the 'same location' and 'spatiotopic' conditions.
source: Bayesian statistics (Benavoli et al., 2014) confirmed that there was overwhelming evidence for an effect in the 'same location' and 'spatiotopic' (posterior probabilities >95%)
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis from Experiment 6.

claim: Bayesian statistics showed no evidence for an effect in the retinotopic or full field conditions.
source: but not in the retinotopic (posterior probability <44.5%) or full field (posterior probability <29.8%) conditions
evidence: This is supported by Bayesian statistical analysis from Experiment 6.

claim: Retinal eccentricity cannot explain the results of Experiment 6.
source: Retinal eccentricity cannot explain our results, since it was matched in the 'same location' and the 'retinotopic' conditions (0 dva), and in the 'spatiotopic' and 'full field' conditions (14 dva), respectively, and thus orthogonal to the factor reference frame.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design of Experiment 6.

claim: Spatiotopy allots the effect to a family of MAEs which are thought to tap into higher-order motion processing stages, such as the positional motion aftereffect.
source: Instead, spatiotopy allots the effect to a family of MAEs which are thought to tap into higher-order motion processing stages, such as the positional motion aftereffect (Turi and Burr, 2012)
evidence: This is inferred from the spatiotopic nature of the effect and comparison to prior work.

claim: The classical MAE occurs in a retinotopic frame of reference.
source: in contrast to the classical MAE, which occurs in a retinotopic frame of reference (Knapen et al., 2009)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The pattern of results in Experiment 6 is predicted by cross-adaptation occurring in a human LIP homolog.
source: This pattern of results is predicted by cross-adaptation occurring in a human LIP homolog.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings in Experiment 6 and knowledge of LIP properties.

claim: The neural circuits recycled to process number retain sensitivity to a visual feature intimately linked to our sense of space, namely motion direction.
source: Taken together, our results show on purely behavioral grounds that the neural circuits recycled to process number retain sensitivity to a visual feature intimately linked to our sense of space, namely motion direction.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all experimental findings.

claim: 'Cortical recycling' expands the original functionality of a circuit instead of replacing it, thus establishing a functional link across domains.
source: This indicates that 'cortical recycling' expands the original functionality of a circuit instead of replacing it, thus establishing a functional link across domains.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all experimental findings.

claim: The combination of tuning function, receptive field size, and frame of reference of the motion direction-numerosity cross-adaptation effect matches the known properties of area LIP neurons.
source: The combination of properties we find in our study, namely the tuning function, receptive field size, and frame of reference of the motion direction-numerosity cross-adaptation effect matches the known properties of area LIP neurons at the first stage of number processing
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and comparison to known LIP properties.

claim: Area LIP neurons are broadly tuned to numerosity.
source: which are broadly tuned to numerosity (Roitman et al., 2007)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Area LIP neurons have relatively small receptive fields.
source: have relatively small receptive fields (Ben Hamed et al., 2001)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Area LIP neurons have a spatiotopic frame of reference.
source: and a spatiotopic frame of reference (Mullette-Gillman et al., 2005)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Neurons in area VIP are narrowly tuned to numerosity.
source: In contrast, neurons in area VIP, the next stage of number processing, are narrowly tuned
evidence: This is established knowledge.

claim: Neurons in area VIP have large receptive fields.
source: and have large receptive fields (Nieder and Dehaene, 2009)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Neurons in area MT have a retinotopic frame of reference.
source: and neurons in area MT, a preceding stage of motion processing, have a retinotopic frame of reference (Born and Bradley, 2005)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A human LIP homolog in the IPS seems to be the most likely origin of the motion direction-numerosity cross-adaptation effect.
source: Hence, a human LIP homolog in the IPS seems to be the most likely origin of the motion direction-numerosity cross-adaptation effect.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and comparison to known properties of different brain areas.

claim: TMS over parietal cortex can disturb number comparisons and motion detection.
source: Motion direction-numerosity cross-adaptation is consistent with studies showing that transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) over parietal cortex can disturb number comparisons and motion detection (Salillas et al., 2009)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The number of items in a display can be overestimated when they move at high speed.
source: as well as those showing that the number of items in a display can be overestimated when they move at high speed (Afraz et al., 2004)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The current study shows that the very same circuits, and not only the same brain area, process number and motion.
source: First, by showing that the very same circuits, and not only the same brain area targeted with TMS, process number and motion
evidence: This is inferred from the cross-adaptation findings.

claim: Sensitivity of number processing extends to a spatial feature that is orthogonal to magnitude, namely motion direction.
source: and second, by showing that sensitivity of number processing extends to a spatial feature that is orthogonal to magnitude, namely motion direction (motion speed is a magnitude itself)
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: Motion direction-numerosity cross-adaption is not simply the consequence of the operation of a 'generalized magnitude processing system'.
source: The latter rules out that motion direction-numerosity cross-adaption is simply the consequence of the operation of a 'generalized magnitude processing system' (Walsh, 2003).
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that motion direction (not a magnitude) affects numerosity.

claim: The results were not effector-dependent.
source: Furthermore, as our results were not effector-dependent
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design.

claim: Number-space associations occur at the level of the representation, not sensorimotor mapping.
source: they strongly suggest that number-space associations occur at the level of the representation, not sensorimotor mapping, which is another function of parietal cortex (Fogassi and Luppino, 2005) and has been invoked as an alternative explanation for number-space associations (Keus and Schwarz, 2005)
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and comparison to alternative explanations.

claim: Moving stimuli can attract attention in their direction of motion.
source: Because moving stimuli can attract attention in their direction of motion (Mattingley et al., 1994; Shi et al., 2010)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: If attention were drawn down the number line during leftward motion adaptation and up the number line during rightward motion adaptation, the consequence would be the opposite pattern of results from what was found.
source: The consequence of this would however be the opposite pattern of results from what we found, namely underestimation after leftward motion (because attention is oriented down the number line) and overestimation after rightward motion (because attention is oriented up the number line).
evidence: This is inferred from theoretical reasoning about attention effects.

claim: Attention is an unlikely explanation for motion direction-numerosity cross-adaptation.
source: Hence, attention is an unlikely explanation for motion direction-numerosity cross-adaptation.
evidence: This is inferred from the pattern of results and control experiments.

claim: The results are indicative of an opponent coding model in which large and small numerosities compete.
source: Our results are indicative of an opponent coding model such as the one proposed for the classical MAE (Mather and Harris, 1998), in which large and small numerosities compete (Figure 6).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings and comparison to theoretical models.

claim: Adaptation causes broadly tuned neurons coding for large numbers to reduce their responsiveness, giving rise to an overshoot in the activity of neurons that code for small numbers, and vice versa, leading to under/overestimation.
source: Here, adaptation causes broadly tuned neurons coding for large numbers to reduce their responsiveness, giving rise to an overshoot in the activity of neurons that code for small numbers, and vice versa, leading to under/overestimation.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation based on the opponent coding model.

claim: The general rightward shift of PSEs in Experiment 1 and the leftward shift of PSEs in Experiment 2 are consistent with previously reported adaptation effects of static numerosity.
source: This is evident in the general rightward shift of PSEs reported in Experiment 1 and the leftward shift of PSEs reported in Experiment 2, and consistent with previously reported adaptation effects of static numerosity (Burr and Ross, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and comparison to prior work.

claim: Leftward motion increases the activity in the small number pool, resulting in increased overestimation after adaptation.
source: leftward motion increases the activity in the small number pool, resulting in increased overestimation after adaptation
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation based on the opponent coding model.

claim: Rightward motion increases the activity in the large number pool, resulting in increased underestimation after adaptation.
source: while rightward motion increases the activity in the large number pool, resulting in increased underestimation after adaptation
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation based on the opponent coding model.

claim: The approximate number sense predicts later mathematical achievement.
source: Finally, it has been shown that the approximate number sense predicts later mathematical achievement (Halberda et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The link between motion and number may open the venue to utilizing motion processing as a marker for number skill development.
source: If the link between motion and number can be further substantiated, it may open the venue to utilizing motion processing as a marker for number skill development (Sigmundsson et al., 2010)
evidence: This is a speculative implication of the findings.

claim: Motion processing could be used to identify children at risk for dyscalculia early in life.
source: and thus to identify children at risk for dyscalculia early in life
evidence: This is a speculative implication of the findings.

claim: The paradigm replicated the well-known numerical distance effect.
source: This paradigm allowed use to investigate motion direction-numerosity cross-adaptation and also replicated the well-known numerical distance effect (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: When comparing numerosities, subjects typically take longer when numerosities are more similar than when they are further apart.
source: When comparing numerosities, subjects typically take longer when numerosities are more similar, i.e., closer to each other on the mental number line, than when they are further apart.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the numerical distance effect.

claim: A parametric rmANOVA on mean reaction times from Experiment 1 revealed a significant effect of test size (F(9,90)=2.834, p=0.006).
source: A parametric rmANOVA on mean reaction times from Experiment 1 revealed a significant effect of test size (F(9,90)=2.834, p=0.006).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of reaction time data.

claim: The numerical distance effect depended on the perceived, not the actual numerosity of the test cloud.
source: Interestingly, the numerical distance effect depended on the perceived, not the actual (green), numerosity of the test cloud, with the longest reaction times around the point of subjective equality (PSE, red), and shorter reaction times the further the test cloud was from that point in either direction.
evidence: This is inferred from analysis of reaction time data in relation to PSE.

claim: Subjects did not perceive attractive or repulsive classical MAEs when incoherently moving dots were presented at the test location.
source: Subjects did not perceive attractive or repulsive classical MAEs when incoherently moving dots were presented at the test location (perceived direction)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the control experiment.

claim: Neither the mean nor the median percent 'same' responses were significantly different from 0 in the aftereffect conditions.
source: Neither the mean nor the median percent 'same' responses were significantly different from 0 in the aftereffect conditions (mean: one sample t-tests, two-sided, all p>0.05; median: percentile bootstrap, all p>0.37)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the control experiment data.

claim: The percentage of 'same' responses did not differ between attractive and repulsive aftereffect conditions.
source: and the percentage of 'same' responses did not differ between attractive and repulsive aftereffect conditions (mean: t(10)=−1.7417, p=0.11, two-sided; median: percentile bootstrap, p>0.38)
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of the control experiment data.

claim: None of the subjects reported perceiving directional motion in the randomly moving test clouds during debriefing after the experiments.
source: In line with these results, none of the subjects reported perceiving directional motion in the randomly moving test clouds during debriefing after the experiments.
evidence: This is supported by subjective reports from participants.

claim: The effect of motion direction on numerosity perception arises in the absence of a classical MAE and thus likely in a different brain area.
source: This indicates that the effect of motion direction on numerosity perception arises in the absence of a classical MAE (like other high-level MAEs, Whitney and Cavanagh, 2003), and thus likely in a different brain area.
evidence: This is inferred from the control experiment results and comparison to prior work.

claim: Current theoretical models of number processing should be expanded to include an opponent process at the analog summation stage.
source: Together, this suggests that current theoretical models of number processing (e.g., Dehaene and Changeux, 1993) should be expanded to include such an opponent process at the analog summation stage
evidence: This is a theoretical implication inferred from the findings.

claim: The link between motion and number may allow utilizing motion processing as a marker for number skill development to identify children at risk for dyscalculia early in life.
source: If the link between motion and number can be further substantiated, it may open the venue to utilizing motion processing as a marker for number skill development (Sigmundsson et al., 2010), and thus to identify children at risk for dyscalculia early in life.
evidence: This is a speculative implication of the findings.
